posts.note: Essay on infidelity and suicide risk; four hedged or general behavioral predictions in the closing paragraphs. 'We need more realism' is normative and was not logged.
Essay on epistemic trust. One borderline implicit adoption claim about hallucinating AI. 'It's going to get better' is discussed as a truism, not logged.
109-word video/podcast blurb; one trivial own-activity intention.

Memoir of a December 2021 ER visit plus the reproduced ER note. Anticipations inside the narrative are past relative to the post date; the ER note's prognosis ('unlikely to benefit from an inpatient admission') is a third party's 2021 statement. No forward-looking claims at the post date.
Substack summer recap. 'One of my hopes for my life is that David makes a movie...' is a wish, not logged.
Podcast blurb; one borderline seasonal claim about bipolar mood changes in the fall. Subscription discount promo not logged.

Guest post by Benjamin Lippmann, DO; the author wrote only the intro and outro. Guest vignettes contain no forecasts. 'Medical science needs time to work out the basis of our psychiatric pathology, yet' is the guest's general observation, not adopted by the author.

Post on the Siddiqi et al. Nature Neuroscience PTSD lesion-network paper and its use at Acacia Clinics and Fermata (author's organizations). Several claims are own-organization; coder may mark CONTROL. 'This is what a better future looks like' and 'That may be a first' are rhetorical/present and not logged.

Post after the Sean Combs indictment, aimed at people in the 'blast radius'. The author explicitly declines to predict the case outcome. 'Some treatments can change how your brain works after trauma in a way that will heal' and 'It can get better' were judged general capability claims/encouragement and not logged.
T-Pain and Cobenfy essay. Cobenfy is described as already out (present fact). Videra Health TD screening tool is described as 'now commercial' (present). No forecasts.

statements.quote: Human sexual behavior beyond what we explicitly agree to in agreements between partners won’t stop— if I had to make a bet.
statements.context: Closing argument of an essay linking infidelity (estimated 20-25% of marriages) to suicide attempts. The author predicts that sexual behavior outside partners' explicit agreements, i.e. infidelity, will not stop, framed as a bet.
statements.confidence_phrase: won’t stop— if I had to make a bet
statements.note: General behavioral prediction with no date or measurable quantity.

statements.quote: the degree to which we choose to acknowledge it, be less sh*tty to each other about it, and the degree to which we work on a cultural context for forgiveness might be able to change. These changes could be lifesaving.
statements.context: Same closing passage, right after the claim that infidelity will not stop. The author contrasts: cultural acknowledgement of infidelity and a context for forgiveness might change, and such change could save lives (reduce infidelity-linked suicides).
statements.confidence_phrase: might be able to change; could be lifesaving
statements.note: Compound hedged claim: cultural change is possible, and it would be lifesaving.

statements.quote: we don't spend time addressing the completely predictable infidelity that will happen in many long-term relationships
statements.context: Final paragraph: couples buy insurance for tiny risks and plan wedding seating but do not plan for infidelity, which the author asserts will happen in many long-term relationships.
statements.note: Base-rate style prediction restating the essay's 20-25% lifetime figures; 'Admit it's likely to happen' repeats it two sentences later.

statements.quote: Planning via uncomfortable conversations could save our partner’s life, our own, or both.
statements.context: Final paragraph: the author claims that agreeing in advance on how partners will talk about likely infidelity could prevent suicides in couples.
statements.note: Conditional, hedged outcome claim tied to the essay's infidelity-suicide link.

statements.quote: This is a good example of why the uptake on AI that hallucinates—or, in human terms, lies to you—misses a key motivation for humans.
statements.context: Essay on epistemic trust (Peter Fonagy's term): people trust messengers rather than messages. The author applies this to AI adoption: AI that hallucinates misses the human need for truth, implying that uptake of such AI will be limited.
statements.note: Borderline: present-tense analysis with an implicit adoption forecast (hallucinating AI will struggle for trust and uptake). Logged for recall.

statements.quote: It gave me a new tool here on Substack, and I’ll use it less-than-polishedly.
statements.context: Short video/podcast post responding to reader feedback on the infidelity column. The author says Substack gave him a new video tool and he intends to keep using it in an unpolished way.
statements.note: Trivial own-newsletter intention; coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: Fall is here. And with it, seasonal changes in mood for those with Bipolar Disorder.
statements.context: Podcast/video blurb titled 'Why Bipolar Depression Gets Worse In The Fall'. Prompted by a friend's reminder that fall has arrived, the author asserts that the season brings mood changes for people with bipolar disorder, the topic of the episode.
statements.note: Borderline: a general clinical pattern stated for the season ahead rather than a dated forecast. Logged for recall.

statements.quote: When the history of how we healed psychiatric illness is written, it will also features my colleague Shan Siddiqui, M.D., a neuropsychiatrist at the Harvard Brain Science Initiative.
statements.context: Post on lesion-network mapping (Mike Fox, human connectome project) and a new TMS target for PTSD. The author predicts that Shan Siddiqi of the Harvard Brain Science Initiative will figure in the eventual history of how psychiatric illness was healed.
statements.horizon_text: When the history of how we healed psychiatric illness is written
statements.note: Legacy/reputation prediction; the quote spells the name 'Siddiqui', elsewhere 'Siddiqi'. It also presupposes that psychiatric illness will be healed.

statements.quote: Suppose we have a PTSD circuit, as hypothesized by lesion information. In that case, it should be possible to stimulate the neurons in that circuit noninvasively to treat PTSD in the same way that accidental brain injuries protect against PTSD.
statements.context: The scientific logic set out before the Nature Neuroscience paper is introduced: lesion mapping in Vietnam veterans suggests a PTSD circuit; if so, noninvasive stimulation (TMS) of that circuit should treat PTSD.
statements.note: Conditional efficacy claim; the post then reports early single-patient results at Acacia and Fermata as confirmation.

statements.quote: It would be some very exciting science, not to mention wildly popular medicine, if this approach works to treat PTSD.
statements.context: Immediately before announcing the Nature Neuroscience paper by Siddiqi and colleagues and the use of the PTSD circuit map by Acacia Clinics (David Carreon). Conditional: if circuit-guided brain stimulation treats PTSD, it becomes wildly popular medicine.
statements.confidence_phrase: would be ... if this approach works
statements.note: Conditional adoption claim about an approach used in the author's own clinics (Acacia, Fermata); coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: By mapping these lesions to a specific brain circuit, the study provides a blueprint for targeting PTSD with non-invasive brain stimulation techniques, such as Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS).
statements.context: Block quote introduced as 'how Acacia's team explains it', describing the study of 193 Vietnam veterans with penetrating brain injuries (Siddiqi et al., Nature Neuroscience). It claims the circuit map is a blueprint for future TMS targeting of PTSD.
statements.note: Borderline: text quoted from Acacia's team (the author's organization) and presented approvingly; forward-looking only by implication. Coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.context: After recounting that he was on the team call when the novel PTSD target was first deployed at Acacia, and that the approach was replicated at his clinic Fermata in New York, the author promises further publications from this work.
statements.note: Own-organization output promise; coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: Other systems need to catch up, but science is not the rate-limiting step this time.
statements.context: Closing line, after 'Welcome to a future of less suffering; it's here now.' and the observation that research findings take 17 years on average to reach practice. The author asserts the science for circuit-guided PTSD treatment is done and that other systems (payers, regulators, clinical practice) will be the bottleneck to spread.
statements.note: Mixed normative/predictive: 'need to catch up' plus a claim about what will limit spread. Borderline; logged for recall.

statements.quote: Those people will be traumatized, squicked out, upset, or something else.
statements.context: Post written after the Sean Combs (Diddy) federal indictment, addressed to people in the fallout. 'Those people' are attendees of Combs' parties, only a portion of which the author imagines were 'Freak-Offs'.
statements.note: General expectation about third parties' emotional reactions; not measurable.

statements.quote: the legal system will adjudicate his guilt or innocence
statements.context: The author declines to speculate on Sean Combs' case ('This article isn't here to speculate on what will happen to Diddy') and states that the legal system will decide his guilt or innocence. Post dated 2024-09-27.
statements.note: Near-truism about the legal process; the author explicitly refuses to predict the outcome.

statements.quote: those who were ensnared and will look back on their roles with regret
statements.context: The author says the post is mainly for those who did nothing wrong, with some thoughts for people ensnared in Combs' alleged conduct, whom he expects to later regret their roles.
statements.note: Expectation about third parties' future feelings; low forecast value.

statements.quote: the strength of victims might waiver in times other than their interactions with law enforcement
statements.context: Reacting to the HSI/DOJ press release praising the 'unwavering strength of victims and witnesses', the author expects victims' strength to waver outside law-enforcement settings, which motivates his six recommendations.
statements.note: Hedged general expectation; 'waiver' is the author's spelling of 'waver'.

statements.quote: so many other options are coming ... It’s a lot in the pipeline
statements.context: Item five of six recommendations ('More than Pills and Talk Therapy Exist'). After listing HOPE-TMS, PRISM fMRI-EEG neurofeedback, Nightware, GammaCore nVNS (stated to be in the FDA Breakthrough process now), Monarch eTNS, stellate ganglion block and ketamine as options 'in the various stages of research and approval', the author says many more trauma treatments are coming, naming research on ibogaine, psilocybin and ultrasound.
statements.note: Pipeline claim for PTSD/trauma treatments with no dates. GammaCore's FDA Breakthrough status is stated as a present fact, not a forecast.
